source_text: Et unde ei aut tanta invidia aut tanta malignitas? Invidia est enim, si ad hoc decepit praecipiendo creaturam suam, ne virtutes eius, in quantum poterat, conaretur imitari; malignitas autem, immo crudelitas, si puniat propter iniusta opera mortales, quae, cum legi eius oboediunt, perpetrarunt.
pass_a_gloss: And whence to him either so great envy or so great malignity? For it is envy if by precepting he deceived his own creature to this end, that it not try, as far as it could, to imitate his virtues; but malignity, nay cruelty, if he punish mortals for unjust works which they perpetrated when they obey his law.

lemmas.lexica: LS creo; Blaise of God as maker

pass_b_english: And where would such envy or malice come from in him? It is envy if he deceived his creature by his commands to prevent it from trying, as far as it could, to imitate his virtues. But it is malice—indeed cruelty—if he punishes mortals for unjust acts they committed by obeying his law.

choices.why: Loaded word in Julian's Latin at this locus; English follows LS/Blaise range without copying NPNF.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
